title: Let Us Make a Name for Ourselves — Brick, Tower, Name
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace be with you. Last lesson we read a register of seventy nations and saw that the many-ness of the peoples is God's own doing. Today the Bible winds the tape back and tells us how those seventy came to be scattered.

And the question this lesson asks may sit closer to home than you expect. Have you ever poured a great deal of effort into something whose real purpose was to make other people remember you? That project you stayed at the office until midnight for. That photograph on social media you picked over so carefully. That line dropped into a gathering — "actually, back in my day I also …"

The people of Babel said something extremely honest — honest enough to be frightening. They said, "Come, let's build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let's make a name for ourselves."

Let me put the answer up front. The sin of Babel was not putting up a building; it was "let's make a name for ourselves." And when God broke them apart, it was not because he was afraid human beings had grown too strong. It was to stop a unity without God from running all the way to the end.
Verse 2: "As they traveled east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they lived there."

Brothers and sisters, take note of that direction — "east", מִקֶּדֶם (*miqedem*). This is the fourth time it comes up in Genesis. In 3:24 the man is driven out of the garden of Eden, and God stations the cherubim on the east side of the garden. In 4:16 Cain goes out from the presence of Yahweh and settles in the land of Nod, east of Eden. In 10:30 the sons of Joktan dwell in the hill country to the east. And now, in chapter 11, they go east again.
In the geography of Genesis, east is the direction of leaving. The author does not have to write "they went far away from God." He only has to write "east", and the reader understands.

And where do they stop? "The land of Shinar", שִׁנְעָר (*Shin'ar*). Brothers and sisters, you saw that place name only last lesson — 10:10 says of Nimrod, "The beginning of his kingdom was Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar." The same ground, the same business. What chapter 10 planted, chapter 11 opens up.
Verse 3: "They said to one another, 'Come, let's make bricks, and burn them thoroughly.' They had brick for stone, and they used tar for mortar."

There is a sound-game in the Hebrew of this verse. "Let's make bricks" is נִלְבְּנָה (*nilbenah*) and "bricks" is לְבֵנִים (*levenim*) — the same root, and read aloud it comes out like a tongue-twister. The author is imitating the noise of a building site at full heat, everybody chanting the same slogan in time.

And there is an important technical detail here: on the Mesopotamian plain there is no stone. So they had to fire their own bricks. Brothers and sisters, that is a great stride in human technology — a manufactured material standing in for a material God made. The text does not say this is sin. The problem is not the brick. The problem is verse 4.
"Traveling east" — why is that a bad thing? Does the direction someone walks in really matter that much?

In Genesis, "east" keeps turning up at the moments when people move away from God. Adam and Eve are driven out, and the cherubim guard the "east" side of the garden of Eden. Cain goes out and settles in the land of Nod, east of Eden. Lot lifts up his eyes, sees the whole plain of the Jordan, and "travels east." So this is not a question of geography; it is a marker in the storytelling — the author uses one direction to flag one kind of movement. That is very useful for the way we read: Scripture often uses a repeated word as a signpost. And the warning it carries for living is this — people rarely leave God by making one great turn. Usually it is a series of small moves, all in the same direction, and only when you look back do you realise how far you have gone.
"Come, let's make bricks" — what is wrong with using a new technology?

Nothing is wrong with technology in itself, and the text does not scold anybody for firing bricks. What you have to notice is the content of those three sentences: "let's make bricks", "let's build ourselves a city, and a tower", "let's make a name for ourselves." The problem is not the brick; it is the purpose in that last sentence, and it is the clause that follows it — "lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth" — which runs exactly counter to the commission God gave humanity, to "replenish the earth." So the test is not the tool but the direction: is the capability in your hands being used to carry out God's commission, or to resist it? The same crane can put up a hospital or put up the tower of Babel. There is only one question that sorts it out: whose name is this for?
2. A Light from the Original: Three Times "Come", Once "Come Down"

Verse 4, the heart of the whole chapter: "They said, 'Come, let's build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let's make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth.'"
There are three things in this verse you have to see clearly.

The first. "A tower whose top reaches to the sky" is וְרֹאשׁוֹ בַשָּׁמַיִם (*verosho vashamayim*), literally "and its head in the heavens." This is not literary exaggeration for "very tall." It is saying that the top of it is to enter God's own territory. The Mesopotamian temple-towers of that age, the ziggurats, were stepped platforms, and their religious function was to be a staircase for a god to come down on. Brothers and sisters, they were not trying to climb up and meet God. They were laying a road so that God would come down at a time of their choosing, to an address of their choosing.

The second. "Let's make a name for ourselves" is נַעֲשֶׂה־לָּנוּ שֵׁם (*na'aseh-lanu shem*), literally "let us make for ourselves a name." "Name", שֵׁם, is one of the words Genesis keeps tracking. In 4:17 Cain calls a city after the name of his son. In 6:4 those men are "men of renown." And now it is "our name."

The third. "Lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth." Brothers and sisters, that sentence flatly contradicts what God commanded in 9:1: "Be fruitful, multiply, and replenish the earth." God says fill the earth; they say let us not be scattered. This is not a technical problem. This is an open move in the opposite direction.
Then verse 5, the sharpest piece of humour in the whole Bible: "Yahweh came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of men built."

"Came down" is וַיֵּרֶד (*vayered*) — he descended. Brothers and sisters, that tower advertised itself as having "its head in the heavens", and God had to come down before he could see it. The author does not jeer at them. He simply sets the two verbs side by side and lets you feel the drop for yourself.

Then in verse 7 God speaks the chapter's third "Come": "Come, let's go down, and there confuse their language." That word, הָבָה (*havah*), is said twice by human beings and once by God. Human beings say, "Come, let's build"; God says, "Come, let's go down." The same shape of sentence, pointing in two completely opposite directions.
Three times "Come" against one "come down" — what is that contrast saying?

Human beings say "Come" three times — הָבָה — come, let's make bricks; come, let's build a city; come, let's make a name. God says it once: "let's go down." In the Hebrew the contrast is very visual. People are piling upward with everything they have, and in God's sight that tower is so small that he has to come down before he can see it. What the text uses is humour, not mockery — what it is dismantling is our illusion that we can reach heaven by our own height. And later the Bible turns this same coming down into good news: that God really did come down, only not to confuse anybody's language. "The Word became flesh and lived among us." So the same action is judgement at Babel and grace at Bethlehem.
3. Confusing the Language: Mercy Inside a Judgement

In verse 6 God says something very interesting: "Behold, they are one people, and they all have one language, and this is what they begin to do. Now nothing will be withheld from them, which they intend to do."

Brothers and sisters, that sentence is often misread as God worrying that human beings had become too strong. It is not that. Read the second half of it slowly: "Now nothing will be withheld from them, which they intend to do."

Picture a human race perfectly of one mind, with nothing standing in its way technically, and of one mind in rebellion — and then ask how far that would go. The twentieth century gave us several examples: a society highly unified, highly mobilised and highly efficient can, in the space of a few years, do the most terrible things in all of human history.

So what is the confusing of the language? It is a brake. When God broke them up, it was not to stop them succeeding; it was to stop them going all the way. This is a judgement — and at the same time it is mercy.

Verse 8: "So Yahweh scattered them abroad from there on the surface of all the earth. They stopped building the city." Brothers and sisters, there is a great deal of weight in those two words, "stopped building." Humanity's first great collective project was abandoned half-finished.

Verse 9: "Therefore its name was called Babel, because there Yahweh confused the language of all the earth. From there, Yahweh scattered them abroad on the surface of all the earth." "Babel", בָּבֶל, means "the gate of God" in Babylonian, while the Hebrew בָּלַל (*balal*) means to confuse. With one play on sound the author rewrites the name they had given themselves: you call this the gate of God; God calls it confusion.
Brothers and sisters, that is where making your own name ends up — the name you leave behind is defined, in the end, by somebody else.
Confusing the language sounds like a punishment, but the sermon calls it mercy. How am I to understand that?

Look at the reason God gives in verse 6: "Behold, they are one people, and they all have one language … Now nothing will be withheld from them, which they intend to do." What a human race under no restraint at all, gathered in one place, with its own name as its aim, would actually do — the twentieth century has already answered that. So scattering them put a far larger catastrophe out of reach. This is common in Scripture: God's obstruction very often looks exactly like frustration. And the practical application is this — when something will not come off no matter what you do, alongside "where am I not trying hard enough?" ask one more question: "could it be that God is blocking this?" But you cannot run it the other way and call every failure God's blocking. That is lazy spiritualising.
Is Pentecost the reversal of Babel? Is there a scriptural basis for saying so?

There is, and it is an echo the early church noticed. At Babel one language becomes many and the people are scattered; at Pentecost people of many languages hear one and the same message and are gathered into one body. Acts 2 goes out of its way to list a dozen or more regional names, and that list is built much the way Genesis 10 is built. But notice this: Pentecost did not take the languages back. God did not make everybody speak Hebrew — he let the gospel go into every language there is. That matters enormously for mission and for the church. Unity is not uniformity; it is not making everyone the same. Unity is different people gathered by one and the same Holy Spirit under one and the same Lord's name.
4. The Lens Narrows: From the Whole Earth to a Single Tent
From verse 10 the tone changes abruptly. A drama played out by the whole human race gives way to a quiet genealogy: "This is the history of the generations of Shem."

This genealogy looks very like the one in chapter 5, but one thing has gone missing — there is no "and he died." In chapter 5 every generation is written up as "all the days of so-and-so were so many years, and he died." In chapter 11 it only says that a man "lived so many years after he became the father of" the next one, "and became the father of more sons and daughters." The author has taken the tolling bell away, because the point of this passage is not death. The point is that the line is now travelling towards one particular man.
Then verse 27: "Now this is the history of the generations of Terah." And into this stretch the author drops several extremely heavy sentences.
Verse 28: "Haran died in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldees, while his father Terah was still alive." — a son dying before his father.

Verse 30: "Sarai was barren. She had no child." Brothers and sisters, please stop at that sentence. Genesis up to this point has said "became the father of" dozens upon dozens of times. The genealogy has been running like a train that never stops. And then, suddenly, one line: "Sarai was barren."
That is a dead stop. The momentum of the whole book comes to a halt right there. And that is precisely the moment at which God opens his mouth.

Verse 31: "Terah took Abram his son … They went from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan. They came to Haran and lived there." Brothers and sisters, look hard at that verse: the destination is Canaan, and the place they actually settle is Haran. Acts 7:2 says that God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran. Which is to say, the call had already gone out back in Ur, and this family got halfway and stopped.
And the place name "Haran" sounds the same as the name of the brother who had died. They stopped in a place loaded with memory — and once they had stopped, they stayed until the father was dead.
"Let's make a name for ourselves" — is wanting to be remembered a sin?

Wanting to be remembered is ordinary to being human, and Scripture nowhere says a person may not achieve anything. The problem is that word "ourselves" in verse 4. The second thing God says to Abram in the very next chapter is, "I will bless you and make your name great." The same thing — but one is seized and the other is given. So the way to tell them apart is very practical: if nobody knew I had done this, would I still do it? If the answer is no, then most likely I am building a tower. And God's way of giving a name very often begins by taking a person somewhere nobody can see him — Joseph, thirteen years from the pit to the palace; Moses, forty years in the wilderness. A name you grabbed you have to keep maintaining yourself. A name God gives needs no maintaining.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching Babel as "technology and civilisation are sin." The problem is not the brick, not the tar, not the building technique. The text does not reproach their competence at any point. The problem is that one clause, "let's make a name for ourselves." If you treat the tool as the sin, your congregation will run away from the world instead of being light inside it.

The second is preaching the confusing of the language as God being afraid people had grown too strong. The point of verse 6 is the direction of that unity, not God's insecurity. What God blocked was a wholeness with no room in it for him — and that is mercy, not jealousy. When you have finished, the impression of God your congregation carries away should be loving and sovereign, not petty.

The third is using Babel to argue against all cooperation and all organisation. The tabernacle later on, the temple, the early church — every one of them was a large-scale joint undertaking. The difference has never lain in how many people or how big the scale, but in who stands at the centre. If the way you preach it leaves your congregation afraid of working together, you have preached it crooked.

The fourth is preaching the judgement and never carrying it through to Pentecost. That list in Acts 2 — "Parthians, Medes, Elamites" — has the skeleton of Genesis 10 underneath it. Without that connection, all this chapter has left is a story about failure. The last picture in this sermon ought to be a crowd hearing its own native language, not an abandoned tower.

The fifth is using the genealogy of chapter 11 to calculate the date of creation. The numbers in this passage differ by well over a thousand years between the Masoretic Text, the Septuagint and the Samaritan Pentateuch, and the Septuagint carries one extra name, Cainan — and Luke 3:36 follows precisely that tradition. Scripture itself has not handed us one uniform sum. A genealogy exists to show a line, not to produce a chronological table.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question. Chinese people care enormously about leaving a name behind — bringing glory to the ancestors, having your name written into history, never disgracing the family. Is that the same thing as Babel's "let's make a name for ourselves"? Brothers and sisters, this one needs a fine discrimination, because the two overlap in part and in part they do not. Caring about your reputation and refusing to bring shame on your family carries a real weight of responsibility inside it, and Proverbs 22:1 does say, "A good name is more desirable than great riches." So there is no need to condemn it wholesale. But the trouble at Babel lies in one word: it is "our" name. Its motive is "lest we be scattered" — which is to say, that name is there to hold off a fear. The way to tell is to ask one question: if nobody knew this was mine, would I still do it? If the answer is no, then what I am making may well be bricks.

The second question. Chinese churches love to talk about "revival", "power", "a grand vision", and we are forever comparing which church has more people and whose meeting was packed out. Does that count as Babel? Let me answer very carefully: not necessarily — but it turns into it very easily. Scale in itself is not sin; three thousand came in on a single day at Pentecost. The real difference lies in three things. First, if this comes off, whose name gets lifted up? Second, are we pursuing growth in order to send people out, or in order that "we not be scattered" — that is, to shore up our own sense of security? Third, do we dare hand our resources over to a church smaller than ours? Brothers and sisters, that third question is the most honest one of all. Anyone willing to give his bricks away for somebody else to build with is not Babel.
When a church runs a large ministry or puts up a big sanctuary, is that building the tower of Babel?

Not necessarily — but this chapter requires us to check three things honestly. First, the purpose: whose name is this for? The preacher's name, the church's name, or the Lord's name? Second, the direction: will this send people out, or fence people in? Babel's aim was "lest we be scattered", and the Great Commission is "go." Third, who carries the cost: are the co-workers being burned dry and families being sacrificed, or is everybody being blessed together? If all three questions pass, the scale itself is not the problem. If one of them fails, the scale will only make the problem grow faster. And remember: a congregation watches what we do, not what we say.
7. Living 321 Out — a Name You Make, or a Name God Gives
Brothers and sisters, let us bring this lesson back to the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — the people of Babel wanted to climb up, and God came down. And Philippians 2:6–7 says of the Lord Jesus that he, "existing in the form of God, didn't consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant." Brothers and sisters, my role model is perfectly clear: the road he walked was the road down, not the road up. And verse 9 says, "Therefore God also highly exalted him" — the order is down first and lifted up afterwards, and it never once runs the other way round.

The Bible is my standard — this chapter lets us see that a person can bring superb execution to something pointed in exactly the wrong direction. They had consensus, they had technique, they had efficiency, they had discipline. Only one thing was wrong: the direction. That is precisely what a standard is for — it is not there to raise your efficiency, it is there to correct your bearing.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — on the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit came down, and every person heard the disciples telling the mighty works of God in his own native tongue. Brothers and sisters, notice this: the Holy Spirit did not standardise the languages back again. He did not cancel the outcome of Babel; he taught the gospel every language there is. The antidote to Babel is not uniformity. It is the unity of the Holy Spirit.

Let Jesus be King — put two sentences side by side. Genesis 11:4, "let's make a name for ourselves"; Genesis 12:2, "I will bless you and make your name great." The same thing, one taken by force and one received from a hand. Letting Jesus be King means giving up the management of your own reputation. And that is extremely concrete. Will you add one more sentence so that something you did gets noticed? When somebody else is being praised, will you slip in the line, "actually, I had a hand in that too"?

Let Jesus receive all the glory — what Babel finally left behind was an abandoned tower and a name somebody else rewrote. And the name God gave Abraham is still being spoken all over the world four thousand years later. Brothers and sisters, a name you fight for gets pulled down. A name God gives does not.

Establish God's system — when God confused the language, what he blocked was a unity without him in it. So God's system does not rest on scale; it rests on who is at the centre. To establish God's system, the first question is always the same one: whose name is this for?

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We have a framework that is very easy to remember — the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal, the eight stages, the four-type diagnosis. A framework is a good thing; it lets truth be remembered, be passed on, be multiplied. But this chapter reminds us of one thing: a body of people with strong consensus, neatly ordered, chanting the same slogan, is not thereby guaranteed to be facing the right way. Babel was the first team in human history with an extremely high level of consensus. So every so often we have to stop and ask one question: this thing we are building right now — does its top reach to the sky, or is it there to make a name for ourselves?
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Tower
Brothers and sisters, one and the same tower of Babel, falling into four kinds of heart, is not seen the same way twice.

The proud heart sees: "Well, at least I am not that worldly." This heart finishes the chapter and starts counting up how many towers other people have built — that man only serves for the sake of his reputation, that church is putting up a kingdom of its own. Brothers and sisters, the sharpest sting in this chapter is that their slogan was "we", and pride's favourite disguise is to leave itself out of the "we".

The fearful heart sees: "What if the things I do are bricks too?" This heart hears a sermon like this and immediately begins interrogating every one of its own motives, and then does not dare do anything at all. To a heart like that I want to say: an impure motive is not a reason to stop, and a motive is never a hundred per cent pure. 1 Corinthians 4:3–4 says, "Yes, I don't even judge my own self. For I know nothing against myself. Yet I am not justified by this, but he who judges me is the Lord." Hand your motives over to him — and then go and do the thing that ought to be done anyway.

The ashamed heart sees: "I will probably leave no name behind at all." You may feel that your whole life has been ordinary — no achievement, no title, nobody to remember you once you are gone. Brothers and sisters, look at this clearly: what this chapter criticises is not leaving something behind, it is who you leave it for. And Luke 10:20 says, "Nevertheless, don't rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven." Your name in that book will last longer than your name on any tower ever built.

The wounded heart sees: "I used to be one of those bricks." You may have been used as a resource in some group — your time, your professional skill, your money, all of it taken to build up somebody else's name, until you were worn down past recognition. Brothers and sisters, let me say this with all seriousness: using people as bricks is Babel's way of working, not God's. In Ezekiel 34 God rebukes in the severest terms those shepherds who look after themselves and not the flock. What wounded you was not God's system. It was somebody who built the wrong tower.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do
First, do one exercise in anonymity. This week do a good turn, and deliberately let nobody know it was you. Afterwards, pay attention to how you feel inside — that feeling will tell you a great deal.

Second, inspect your three "bricks." Write down the three things you have put the most of yourself into this season, and beside each one write an honest sentence: if nobody knew this was mine, would I still do it?

Third, when somebody else is being praised, practise not adding that line. If an opening comes this week to say "actually, I had a hand in that too", deliberately do not say it. You will discover how hard that one second is — and you will find out how tall that tower stands inside you.

Fourth, pray once for a community whose language and background are not yours. The antidote to Babel is Pentecost. Move your heart across from "lest we be scattered" to "to the uttermost parts of the earth."

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. The Bible records a group of people building a tower to reach heaven, and their stated reason was very honest — "let's make a name for ourselves." And that tower, which advertised its top as being in the sky, the Bible says God had to come down to see. So I learned one thing: the height a person climbs to with everything he has is, in God's sight, a size you have to stoop down to look at.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I will no longer make a name for myself; my name is to come from God, and not out of my own hand.
I declare that I will walk the road that goes down, because my Lord walked that road first.
I declare that I will not use people as bricks; what I hold precious is people, not the project.
I declare that I will replenish the earth and refuse "lest we be scattered"; my security is in God, not in a circle of my own.
Doing "one thing this week that nobody knows I did" — does that not just turn into playacting?

If the motive is "I want to prove to myself how humble I am", then yes, it becomes another kind of performance. So keep it small and very ordinary: refill something everybody uses, push somebody's chair back in, do one thing for a person that he will never find out about. When it is done, do not write it down and do not go back over it; just let it pass. The purpose of this is not self-cultivation, it is calibration — it lets you experience for yourself, once, that a good thing nobody knows about is still good. And that is precisely the antidote to Babel. If a sense of grievance surfaces while you are doing it — "and nobody even saw" — that is fine too. That is the very moment you find out how high your own tower has got.
Brothers and sisters, if this lesson may leave only one comparison behind, I want it to be two ladders.
In chapter 11, human beings put up a tower meant to reach heaven. The building stopped, the name was rewritten as "confusion", and the people were scattered over the whole earth.

And in chapter 28 there is a man on the run who falls asleep out in open country with a stone for a pillow. He dreams of a ladder set up on the earth, with its top reaching to heaven, and the angels of God on it, going up and coming down.

Brothers and sisters, both of them join heaven and earth. One was built by human beings and it failed; one was let down by God and it held. And in John 1:51 the Lord Jesus says to Nathanael, "Most certainly, I tell you all, hereafter you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man."
He replaced that ladder with himself.

So the road to heaven was never one we put up ourselves. If you are still labouring away at accumulating enough — good enough, qualified enough, weighty enough — this chapter has something to say to you: that road has already been let down, and it has a name.

And there is one more thing I want you to see. This chapter ends by stopping at Haran. A family set out for Canaan, settled down halfway, and stayed there until the father died. Brothers and sisters, a great many people's obedience looks just like that — it is not that they refuse to go, it is that halfway there they put up a house. God will speak again, but you have to be willing to move again. And the very first sentence of the next chapter is this: "Now Yahweh said to Abram, 'Leave your country …'"

The focus is not on how high I built, not on how many people remember my name, and not on where I stopped. The focus is on Jesus — he is the Lord who came down from heaven and then became the ladder himself. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us this week: to put down the brick in our hand, and to set out from Haran one more time. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at the level of mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★ Human beings say "Come" three times; God says "let's go down" once. What is that contrast saying?
2. ★★★ "Let's make a name for ourselves", and God saying in the next chapter, "I will bless you and make your name great" — where does the difference lie, and how would you test for it?

3. ★ Their reason for building the city was "lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth", and the commission God gave humanity was to "replenish the earth." How does that help us tell a true vision from a false one?
4. ★★ Pentecost did not take the languages back; it let the gospel go into every language there is. What correction does that make to our definition of "unity"?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I mean to leave something behind), fearful (afraid of being forgotten), ashamed (I have never got anything done), wounded (what I did had somebody else's name put on it). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "I will bless you and make your name great." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there something on your plate right now about which you would say, "if nobody knew I had done it, I would not much want to do it"? What is the longing underneath that thing?
8. ★ Finish it in one sentence: "What I most want other people to remember me for is …"
9. ★★ This week you are to do one thing that nobody knows you did. Name that thing, and promise the group: once it is done, you will not talk about it.

Leader's reminder: question seven will touch old wounds where somebody's credit was taken from them. If anyone brings up something that happened inside the church, do not adjudicate the rights and wrongs of it on the spot; follow up with him privately afterwards.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ At home this week, is there something in which you will hand the credit over to another person?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or at school, in which meeting will you name somebody else's name before your own?

12. ★★★ The practice of three questions: this week, before you take on anything new, ask first "whose name is this for?", "will this send people out or fence people in?" and "who does the cost fall on?" Name the one decision you have coming up.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and ask him to check on the seventh day whether you did that thing nobody knows about. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, there is a group of people in the Bible who built a tower, and their aim was to make a name for themselves. Second, God came down and confused their speech, and the result was that people filled the whole earth after all. Third, so now, before I do anything, I am learning to ask one question first: whose name is this for? Write down now who you will tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the thing nobody will know about that you are doing this week, and who you will tell. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to pull down the tower inside us that we built for our own name.
